regeln: Within each spoken phase use multiple distinct relevant shots, roughly 3-5 seconds each for Shorts; long videos can allow purposeful longer demonstrations. Preserve continuous narration and accurate subtitle timing.
A zoom, crop, subtitle change or decorative background does not count as a new motif. Never fill missing images with candles, unrelated stock or background-only frames.
Show the main image prominently; avoid tiny repeated photos in a mostly empty vertical frame. Preserve genuine evidence and important image details.
For AI Tools Explained identify the exact tool briefly, then show genuine interface views and different source-supported examples. Never present stock or an illustration as a real tool result.
Use original urban painted open-world-game poster styling for fictional scenes and presenters; no copied game characters. Match narrated action and era.

Clear speech and readable captions alone do not make a professional video. Inspect useful motif changes and narration-image alignment over the entire video. Missing main imagery is a substantial defect.
Include mandatory spoken like, share and save calls at the correct format-specific positions. Do not replace this requirement with a different CTA.

AI Tools Explained is for viewers with a practical task. Do not read parameter counts, architecture names, pipeline tags, context lengths or benchmark claims as a substitute for useful explanation. Explain the human task, the source-supported action and a concrete limit. A generic trending-tools question failed story review twice; prefer a specific visual workflow.

The user confirmed original presenter references on 2026-10-05: Business Origin Stories uses the blue-eyed man with a fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch; AI Tools Explained uses the black-haired man with black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses. Preserve identity and typical clothing, vary action and setting.

Introduce the correct presenter at the opening and bring that same presenter back during the video in useful actions. Do not confine the figure to the ending. Do not replace original channel figures with different fictional people; anonymous period workers remain clearly illustrative supporting people, never a real-founder likeness.

Prefer vivid original painted open-world-game scenes to long holds on lifeless documentary photos. Preserve factual accuracy and show authentic tool examples briefly as evidence. Camera moves alone are not new motifs or full character animation.

The user confirmed on 2026-10-05 that both new delivered videos are much better than before. Preserve the original painted world, recurring channel identity, matching main imagery, music and useful scene changes. The long-term quality target remains 10/10; the user did not give these videos a numeric score. Do not replace their actual AI scores or the existing 7/10 delivery threshold with the aspirational target.

belege.text:
Official Anthropic Claude (Claude Code) documentation/help page (https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/claude-code-best-practices).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Best practices for Claude Code - Claude Code Docs
Fetch the complete documentation index at: /docs/llms.txt
Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
Responses are generated using AI and may contain mistakes.
Claude Code is built in a way that, in most cases, your first plain prompt in a fresh session already does the right thing, without any setup on your part.
To let commands run without you approving each one, new terminal and VS Code sessions start in auto mode .
To keep your main conversation focused while independent work happens in parallel, Claude delegates to subagents and checks in only when it has to.
To keep a long session going without you managing it, your conversation is compacted automatically before the context window fills.
This page covers what to do when the defaults aren’t enough. That usually happens when your project has knowledge, rules, or constraints that Claude can’t see from the code alone:
A deploy process that lives in someone’s head
A file that must never be read
A check that has to pass before anything counts as done
A budget you need to stay under
No default can know those things about your project, so this is where a small amount of setup on your side pays off.
When a session doesn’t go the way you expected, it’s almost always one of these:
Claude built something different from what you had in mind, or it has to rediscover the same fact at the start of every session. It’s missing information it can’t get from reading the repo. See Tell Claude what it can’t see .
Claude said it was done and it wasn’t quite, usually because it had no way to check its own work. See Give Claude a check to run .
Claude did something that must never happen in this repo, or skipped a step that must always happen. A prompt alone can’t guarantee either of those. See Enforce the rules that can’t have exceptions .
Claude got it right, but it took more time, tokens, or permission prompts than the task was worth. See Change a default .
Let Claude run without you applies the same four points to unattended runs, and What you can stop doing lists the advice that current models have made unnecessary.
Setup for a whole team is on a separate page: Set up Claude Code for your organization .
Every instruction you give Claude Code is one of these:
Non-deterministic: you write the instruction, and Claude (the model) reads it. This can be your prompt, CLAUDE.md , or a skill. The model then decides what to do with this information. It usually follows your commands, and current models are good at understanding your intent without much context, but there’s no guarantee that it’ll follow your instructions.
Deterministic: you configure the instruction, and Claude Code (the harness) has to execute this. This can be a hook, a deny rule, or a managed setting. Claude Code applies this every time, no matter what the model decided to do.
Most things in Claude Code come in both forms:
Non-deterministic (Claude decides) Deterministic (Claude Code enforces)
What to do Your prompt, CLAUDE.md , skills Claude picks up itself Hooks, and which skills only you can start
What it can touch Auto mode’s classifier Deny rules, the sandbox in strict mode , managed settings
When it’s done A request for evidence, /goal , /code-review Tests, typecheck, a Stop hook, CI
How much it spends Effort level, Claude’s own pace --max-turns or --max-budget-usd with -p , a spend limit you’ve set
Who has the last word Claude’s summary of what it did Branch protection, a person who approves the merge
Most of the time, you want Claude to decide. Almost every guideline has exceptions, and current models are good at reading the code in front of them and judging whether a guideline fits the situation. With the actual code in front of it, Claude is usually better placed to make that call than a rule you wrote in advance.
The deterministic kind is for when you want to make sure certain things always happen (or never happen), no matter what the model decides. This doesn’t have to be anything dramatic. Auto mode already blocks the dramatic things , like a production deploy or a force push over someone’s work. It’s usually something specific to your project, and it can be as niche as you want it to be:
Never edit the generated client in src/gen/
Always run the license-header script after creating a file
You could’ve written either of these as a line in CLAUDE.md or in your prompt, and Claude would follow it nearly every time. But no matter how strongly you word it, whether Claude follows that line on a given turn is still Claude’s call.
If you keep adding emphasis to a CLAUDE.md line and Claude still misses it, that’s a sign the line belongs in a hook. The reverse holds too: if you have hooks for things that are only preferences, delete them and let Claude decide.
Tell Claude what it can’t see
Only write down what Claude can’t find by reading the repo, or what it would otherwise spend time rediscovering every session.
Claude starts every task by reading your code, and current models are very good at this. They’ll find your file layout, your conventions, your test framework, and how existing components are built, usually faster than you could explain them. That means Claude already knows most of what you might be tempted to write down for it.
What it can’t find is the information that was never in the repo:
A decision your team made in a meeting
A deploy process that lives in one person’s head
The environment variable your integration tests need
There’s also information that is in the repo but takes a few minutes of digging to find, and Claude has to redo that digging at the start of every session.
A good test before you write anything down for Claude:
Could it find this by reading the code?
Would it actually go and look?
If both are yes, leave it out.
A specific prompt helps for the same reason, because it gives Claude information it doesn’t already have. If you name the file, describe the symptom, and say what “fix

belege.name: Anthropic Claude (Claude Code) official guide
belege.text:
Official Anthropic Claude (Claude Code) documentation/help page (https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/overview).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Fetch the complete documentation index at: /docs/llms.txt
Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
Responses are generated using AI and may contain mistakes.
Claude Code is an AI-powered coding assistant that helps you build features, fix bugs, and automate development tasks. It understands your entire codebase and can work across multiple files and tools to get things done.
Claude Code runs on several surfaces: the terminal, IDE extensions, a desktop app, and the web. Choose one from the tabs below to get started. Most surfaces require a Claude subscription or Anthropic Console account. The Terminal CLI, VS Code, and JetBrains also support third-party providers .
The full-featured CLI for working with Claude Code directly in your terminal. Edit files, run commands, and manage your entire project from the command line. To install Claude Code, open a terminal and run the command for your system. If you haven’t used a terminal before, the terminal guide shows how to open one and paste the command.
On Windows, your prompt shows PS C:\ when you’re in PowerShell and C:\ without the PS when you’re in CMD. Windows PowerShell:
irm https: // claude.ai / install.ps1 | iex
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.cmd -o install.cmd && install.cmd && del install.cmd
The install command shows no progress while it downloads Claude Code. When the installer finishes, open a new terminal window and run claude --version . A working installation prints a version number. If your shell says claude isn’t found or isn’t recognized, the install directory isn’t on your PATH yet: see Fix your PATH . If you see The token '&&' is not a valid statement separator , you’re in PowerShell, not CMD. If you see 'irm' is not recognized as an internal or external command , you’re in CMD, not PowerShell. If the install command fails with syntax error near unexpected token '<' , a 403 , or any other error, see Troubleshoot installation to match the error to a fix and for alternative install methods. Git for Windows is recommended on native Windows so Claude Code can use the Bash tool. If Git for Windows is not installed, Claude Code uses PowerShell as the shell tool instead. WSL setups do not need Git for Windows.
Native installations automatically update in the background to keep you on the latest version.
Homebrew offers two casks. claude-code tracks the stable release channel, which is typically about a week behind and skips releases with major regressions. claude-code@latest tracks the latest channel and receives new versions as soon as they ship.
Homebrew installations do not auto-update. Run brew upgrade claude-code or brew upgrade claude-code@latest , depending on which cask you installed, to get the latest features and security fixes.
WinGet installations do not auto-update. Run winget upgrade Anthropic.ClaudeCode periodically to get the latest features and security fixes. You can also install with apt, dnf, or apk on Debian, Fedora, RHEL, and Alpine. Then start Claude Code in any project. Replace your-project with the path to a project directory on your machine:
Claude Code prompts you to log in on first use. If you’ve set the ANTHROPIC_API_KEY environment variable and you approve the key when Claude Code asks whether to use it, Claude Code skips the login prompt. Continue with the Quickstart →
See advanced setup for installation options, manual updates, or uninstallation instructions. Visit installation troubleshooting if you hit issues.
The VS Code extension provides inline diffs, @-mentions, plan review, and conversation history directly in your editor.
Or search for “Claude Code” in the Extensions view ( Cmd+Shift+X on Mac, Ctrl+Shift+X on Windows/Linux). After installing, open the Command Palette ( Cmd+Shift+P / Ctrl+Shift+P ), type “Claude Code”, and select Open in New Tab . Get started with VS Code →
A standalone app for running Claude Code outside your IDE or terminal. Review diffs visually, run multiple sessions side by side, schedule recurring tasks, and start cloud sessions. Download and install:
On Ubuntu or Debian, where the app is in beta, install it with apt by following the Linux install instructions
After installing, launch Claude, sign in, and click the Code tab to start coding. The app includes Claude Code, so you don’t need to install the CLI separately. A paid subscription is required. Learn more about the desktop app →
Run Claude Code in your browser with no local setup. Kick off long-running tasks and check back when they’re done, work on repos you don’t have locally, or run multiple tasks in parallel. For a longer body of work, create a project and let Claude coordinate the parallel sessions for you. Available on desktop browsers and the Claude app for iOS and Android . Start coding at claude.ai/code . Get started →
A plugin for IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm, and other JetBrains IDEs with interactive diff viewing and selection context sharing. Install the Claude Code plugin from the JetBrains Marketplace and restart your IDE. The plugin requires the Claude Code CLI, installed separately; see the JetBrains setup steps . Get started with JetBrains →
Here are some of the ways you can use Claude Code:
Automate the work you keep putting off
Claude Code handles the tedious tasks that eat up your day: writing tests for untested code, fixing lint errors across a project, resolving merge conflicts, updating dependencies, and writing release notes.
claude "write tests for the auth module, run them, and fix any failures"
Describe what you want in plain language. Claude Code plans the approach, writes the code across multiple files, and verifies it works. For bugs, paste an error message or describe the symptom. Claude Code traces the issue through your codebase, identifies the root cause, and implements a fix. See common workflows for more examples.
Claude Code works directly with git. It stages changes, writes commit messages, creates branches, and opens pull requests.

Official Anthropic Claude (Claude Code) documentation/help page (https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/mcp).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Connect Claude Code to tools via MCP - Claude Code Docs
Fetch the complete documentation index at: /docs/llms.txt
Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further.
Responses are generated using AI and may contain mistakes.
Claude Code can connect to hundreds of external tools and data sources through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) , an open source standard for AI-tool integrations. MCP servers give Claude Code access to your tools, databases, and APIs.
Connect a server when you find yourself copying data into chat from another tool, like an issue tracker or a monitoring dashboard. Once connected, Claude can read and act on that system directly instead of working from what you paste.
If you’re connecting your first server, start with the MCP quickstart for a step-by-step walkthrough. This page is the full reference.
What you can do with MCP
With MCP servers connected, you can ask Claude Code to:
Implement features from issue trackers : “Add the feature described in JIRA issue ENG-4521 and create a PR on GitHub.”
Analyze monitoring data : “Check Sentry and Statsig to check the usage of the feature described in ENG-4521.”
Query databases : “Find emails of 10 random users who used feature ENG-4521, based on our PostgreSQL database.”
Integrate designs : “Update our standard email template based on the new Figma designs that were posted in Slack”
Automate workflows : “Create Gmail drafts inviting these 10 users to a feedback session about the new feature.”
React to external events : an MCP server can also act as a channel that pushes messages into your session, so Claude reacts to Telegram messages, Discord chats, or webhook events while you’re away.
Browse reviewed connectors in the Anthropic Directory . Directory connectors use the same MCP infrastructure as Claude Code, so you can add any remote server listed there with claude mcp add .
Verify you trust each server before connecting it. Servers that fetch external content can expose you to prompt injection risk .
To build your own server, see the MCP server guide for protocol fundamentals and the Claude connector building docs for authentication, testing, and Directory submission.
You can also have Claude scaffold a server for you with the official mcp-server-dev plugin .
In the VS Code extension or the desktop app, follow Install a plugin instead of this step. In a terminal, start Claude Code by running claude , then enter this at its prompt:
If the install fails, match the message Claude Code reports:
Marketplace "claude-plugins-official" not found : add the marketplace with /plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-official , then retry the install.
Plugin "<name>" not found in marketplace "claude-plugins-official" : your local copy of the marketplace catalog may be out of date. Refresh it with /plugin marketplace update claude-plugins-official , then retry the install. If the retry prints the same message, see Plugin not found in marketplace .
If the install summary reports Run /reload-plugins to apply. , Claude Code then runs that reload for you. If the reload warns that your next message would re-read the conversation, run /reload-plugins --force .
Claude asks about your use case and scaffolds a remote HTTP or local stdio server.
MCP servers can be configured in several ways depending on your needs:
Option 1: Add a remote HTTP server
HTTP servers are the recommended option for connecting to remote MCP servers. This is the most widely supported transport for cloud-based services.
claude mcp add --transport http < nam e > < ur l >
# Real example: Connect to Notion
claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
claude mcp add --transport http secure-api https://api.example.com/mcp \
When configuring MCP servers via JSON in .mcp.json , ~/.claude.json , or claude mcp add-json , the type field accepts streamable-http as an alias for http . The MCP specification uses the name streamable-http for this transport, so configurations copied from server documentation work without modification.
A JSON entry that has a url but no type is a configuration error, because Claude Code reads an entry with no type as a stdio server. Claude Code skips that server and reports MCP server "<name>" has a "url" but no "type"; add "type": "http" (or "sse" / "ws") to this entry .
Only an SDK host application, such as an Agent SDK application or the desktop app , can register an in-process "type": "sdk" server. Claude Code skips a "type": "sdk" entry in .mcp.json , ~/.claude.json , or settings and reports Skipped — MCP server "<name>" declares type "sdk", which only an SDK host application can register .
In --output-format stream-json runs, Claude Code also reports a skipped --mcp-config entry in the system/init event’s mcp_server_errors field , so scripts can detect that the server never loaded.
Option 2: Add a remote SSE server
The SSE (Server-Sent Events) transport is deprecated. Use HTTP servers instead, where available.
Some services still expose only an SSE endpoint. Add these with the same claude mcp add --transport http <name> <url> command as an HTTP server . Claude Code tries the HTTP transport first and switches to SSE when the server doesn’t accept it. The automatic switch requires Claude Code v2.1.265 or later.
On an earlier version, or to connect over SSE directly, pass --transport sse instead:
claude mcp add --transport sse < nam e > < ur l >
# Real example: Connect to Asana
claude mcp add --transport sse asana https://mcp.asana.com/sse
claude mcp add --transport sse private-api https://api.company.com/sse \
Option 3: Add a local stdio server
Stdio servers run as local processes on your machine. They’re ideal for tools that need direct system access or custom scripts.
